selectionSummary: Consistent world-impact criteria: cross-border scale, breadth of affected populations, long-term consequences for security, climate and economic systems, and corroboration by separate originating newsrooms. The three stories are an editorial selection, not a quantitative ranking.

snapshot.summary: COP31 finished without a global cover decision, a Russian corvette was almost submerged in a suspected drone attack in Libya, and international tanker traffic remained at risk around the contested Strait of Hormuz. In each story, verifiable events were separated from unresolved military or diplomatic claims.
connections: Disputes about who sets the rules shaped global climate cooperation, port sovereignty in Libya and access to vital sea lanes.
Assertions of good-faith negotiation, lawful military logistics and safe maritime control were contested by other actors.
A gap remained between official explanations and independent evidence of causes, policy outcomes or legal responsibility.
uncertainties: Climate negotiations remained without an overarching agreement while some narrower initiatives proceeded.
The Benghazi attacker, alleged launch location and complete casualty toll were unconfirmed at November 22 cutoff.
Whether named tankers had hit mines or been struck by projectiles, and the legality of Iran's restrictions, were unsettled.

stories.title: COP31 ends without overarching deal after fossil-fuel deadlock
stories.summary: COP31 concluded on November 22 without a consensus decision on its main Antalya pact after talks ran into Sunday. The EU and other governments objected to draft wording that omitted a direct fossil-fuel transition commitment, while Türkiye's presidency said it had pursued every workable compromise. Several separate initiatives and narrower decisions survived; the core political pact did not.
stories.whyItMatters: The collapse affects multilateral coordination on emissions, climate-finance commitments and investment signals affecting populations and economies worldwide. Existing climate agreements were not erased.
stories.selectionRationale: Worldwide, multi-generational implications for climate and energy investment, alongside failure of the main international political agreement.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters' original listed 23:40 UTC Nov21 is after local midnight on Nov22. The Guardian original Nov22 13:54 CET converts to 12:54 UTC; Anadolu provides a Nov22 date without timezone precision. All have independent originating reporters. Reuters displays an undated current update indicator; no archived cutoff capture was verified.

commonFacts.text: COP31 closed on November 22 without adoption of an overarching climate cover decision.
EU delegates rejected the proposed pact because it did not explicitly name fossil fuels.
Türkiye's COP president Murat Kurum said no consensus had been reached and that the presidency had sought compromise.
Fossil-fuel wording, climate finance and the role of carbon-removal technologies were contentious.

framingDifferences.text: Central disputed question: Accept a compromise cover pact lacking explicit fossil-fuel transition language, or reject it as too weak? Position A: Kurum, reported by cop22-a, said countries needed flexibility to obtain a workable collective result. Position B: EU minister O'Brien, reported by cop22-g, said omitting fossil fuels was unacceptable and risked greenwashing. The reference cop22-r corroborates the omission and failure, but neither source proves which strategy would yield better future emissions.

Competing explanations of collapse remain attributed: Kurum faulted insufficient concessions by some parties; European objectors said the draft failed to address the central driver of climate change. All sources confirm nonadoption; no evidence establishes a single actor's sole responsibility.

uncertainties: Whether future negotiations will explicitly commit governments to fossil-fuel reductions and specific adaptation financing remained undecided.
Realized emissions benefits of pledges and carbon-removal technology cannot be inferred from draft wording.
Later live-page edits may not reproduce the exact historical cutoff text.

unverifiedClaims.text: Kurum said Türkiye exhausted all possible avenues to consensus and other states were insufficiently flexible.
unverifiedClaims.reason: Official assessment of diplomatic responsibility, not independently proven as an exhaustive causal account.

unverifiedClaims.text: Delegates and activists characterized the abandoned draft as greenwashing fossil fuels.
unverifiedClaims.reason: Attributed evaluative description rather than a separately established factual finding.

stories.title: Suspected drone attack nearly sinks Russian corvette in Benghazi, Libya
stories.summary: An explosion aboard the Russian Navy corvette Merkury in Benghazi on November 22 was investigated as a suspected sea-drone attack; satellite imagery showed much of the vessel submerged. The eastern Libyan government said it had permission to refuel and called the strike an intrusion. The western Tripoli administration, while rejecting proxy warfare, also objected to foreign military use of Libyan ports. Who launched the drones was not established at cutoff.
stories.whyItMatters: The war between Russia and Ukraine appeared to pose new risks to North Africa, Libya's divided sovereignty and the Mediterranean's military and commercial maritime traffic.
stories.selectionRationale: Serious loss of a Russian military asset outside its main theatre, with implications for third-country sovereignty and civilian shipping.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters documented Vantor imagery and medical sources; Al Jazeera adds independent Benghazi local reporting; The Kyiv Independent provides an original bylined comparison and quotes Tripoli's public statement, although AP-origin military-source details are clearly identified as such. Unverified death, cargo and drone-origin allegations are not counted as established.

commonFacts.text: The Russian Navy corvette Merkury suffered grave damage at Benghazi on November 22 and satellite imagery showed it largely capsized or submerged.
The eastern administration said it had permitted the ship to refuel and resupply under Russia-Libya cooperation and that a drone strike was suspected.
Libyan authorities in both east and west warned about being drawn into external conflicts, while identifying different underlying hazards.
No one had publicly claimed responsibility for the suspected Benghazi attack by the November 22 reporting cutoff.

framingDifferences.text: Central disputed question: Is the principal Libyan sovereignty violation an attack on a ship legally permitted to resupply, or using Libyan ports for foreign military logistics? Position A: eastern authorities (lib22-j) condemned the suspected assault and said Russian refuelling was permitted. Position B: Tripoli's government (lib22-k) objected to military/logistical use of Libyan ports exposing the country to proxy war. Both condemned foreign spillover, so this is a difference in identified responsibility and remedial priorities, not opposite attitudes to civilian safety. lib22-r confirms the underlying official statements, not their legal conclusions.

Evidence assessment: satellite imagery supports the physical near-sinking, but neither the suspected Ukrainian launch site, the ship's reported cargo nor a legal justification for any attack was independently established. Assertions about drone origins are not proof against western Libya or Ukraine.

uncertainties: Who launched the drones and where they came from were unresolved at cutoff; later acknowledgements are outside this edition.
The true casualty total and alleged cargo of arms and drones were not reliably reconciled.
The scope and findings of a proposed international investigation and effects on Libyan security were not yet known.

unverifiedClaims.text: Eastern Libyan military sources suspected Ukrainian sea drones launched from western Libya.
unverifiedClaims.reason: No official claim of responsibility or independent forensic confirmation existed by cutoff.

unverifiedClaims.text: Al Jazeera local contacts alleged deaths and weapons cargo, while Reuters medical sources described ten minor injuries.
unverifiedClaims.reason: The accounts were not independently reconciled; changing or incomplete casualty estimates are not a manufactured ideological dispute.

stories.title: Hormuz shipping remains hazardous as Iran disputes responsibility for tanker fires
stories.region: Strait of Hormuz / Oman and Iran
stories.summary: Commercial vessels remained in danger around the Strait of Hormuz through November 22 amid US-Iran hostilities. British maritime monitors described unidentified projectiles striking tankers near Oman; Iranian officials reported other tanker fires after alleged mine strikes in prohibited areas. The ships and mechanisms were not independently reconciled. Iran's demand for prior routing permission contrasts with outside reporting that treats its tightening control of transit as a deliberate coercive strategy.
stories.whyItMatters: The strait historically carried close to one-fifth of global crude-oil supply; disruption threatens multinational seafarers, ecosystems, export revenues and global energy costs.
stories.selectionRationale: Persisting international supply-route risk and direct confrontation over transit access in the world's central Gulf oil chokepoint.
stories.evidenceNote: Three independently originating newsrooms: Reuters incident report Nov20, Tasnim Iranian-army reporting Nov20, and Al Jazeera news Nov21 incorporating its own Tehran correspondent as well as disclosed AFP/Reuters inputs. All first-published within 72 hours of Nov22 cutoff; reports from distinct unidentified vessels are deliberately not conflated.

commonFacts.text: British maritime authorities reported tanker projectile incidents near Oman while Iranian military sources reported tanker fires attributed to mines in the Strait of Hormuz period.
Iranian authorities require operators to coordinate and use military-designated routes in the strait, according to their own statements.
Threats to commercial ships continued in a US-Iran confrontation affecting a waterway that previously handled roughly one-fifth of global oil trade.
The reporting did not establish identical vessel identities linking British projectile observations to Iranian mine assertions.

framingDifferences.text: Central disputed question: Are tanker hazards mainly caused by crews violating Iranian protective routes, or by Iran's coercive restriction of international passage? Position A: Iranian navy, reported by hor22-t, blames tankers that allegedly ignore safety rules and says Iranian authorization is required. Position B: Al Jazeera's own Tehran correspondent, documented in hor22-j, interprets Tehran's restrictions as deliberately escalating maritime pressure in response to the US blockade. hor22-r confirms the independently reported hazard but not either causal generalization or Iran's claimed legal authority.

The route-enforcement and maritime-monitoring accounts do not establish a definitive 'mine versus projectile' conflict for a single named ship: different incident dates and unconfirmed identities prevent that inference. The genuine policy divergence is whether unilateral Iranian control improves safety or intentionally threatens maritime commerce.

uncertainties: The identities, precise locations and causes of individual damaged vessels were unverified across reports.
Whether ships disabled their navigation equipment and whether mines caused specific fires were unresolved.
Safe transit and a diplomatic settlement of the US-Iran maritime confrontation had no confirmed timetable.

unverifiedClaims.text: Iran's navy said tanker crews disabled identification systems, crossed prohibited routes and hit mines.
unverifiedClaims.reason: No selected independent vessel or explosive forensics verifies those military allegations.

unverifiedClaims.reason: This is an attributed military-statement tally, not independently audited incident volume.
